utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I think we are still continuing with your examination, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your submission. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Grant Niemann, I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Turone, Ms McHenry and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, my name is Zeljko Olujic, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I am an attorney from Croatia. Appearing with me is my colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear here with Ms Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry for the short forgetfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might we have document 124 on the screen, please. Your Honours, prior to the adjournment on Friday I had reached document 124, which is now on the screen. Your Honours, I had started to go through this document in order to make submissions about why it is that we submit that it is a reliable document and ought to be admitted into evidence. Your Honours will recall, this is a report and it was found on the premises of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honours, we seem to be having a little problem with Mr. Karabdic's translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: It is better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It has apparently been solved. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It has improved his English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the centre paragraph of that document, which commences with the words, "in the course of the day of 25th October 1992", there is a reference there to the fact that there was a warning of an attempt to assassinate and then, a little further down, there is a mention of the time, 1800 hours, and, "the two sniper bullets whizzed past my head and shoulders". I have already taken your Honours to references to that. Your Honours, into the next paragraph there is a reference, in the next paragraph, starting, "of course I knew", et cetera, in the last sentence there: "It is unfortunate that position is too well known to the HVO general staff. We believe that I am the only remaining hurdle to the achievement of this goal." Your Honours, in our submission this relates to the continued and -- the continued state of animosity that started to grow between the HVO and the BH army in the Konjic area, and particularly in which the accused, Mr. Delalic, was involved and has spoken of in other parts of the evidence. There are numerous references to this, your Honours, in other documents, and your Honours have also heard it in the evidence of General Pasalic. One particular document where it is mentioned is document 126, and if the first page of that document could please be put on to the screen now. The very bottom paragraph is the paragraph which I am referring to. This is a memorandum addressed to the main staff of the supreme command. It is dated 27th April 1993. There is a reference to the HVO in paragraph 2 at the bottom there, where the author says: "The Konjic army command believes that the only one HVO company from the villages of Trija and Birja crossed over to the Chetnik side because they were no longer there." It goes on to make reference to the night the HVO forces crossed the lake. If we can go into the last page of that document, page 6, at the very top of the page, under paragraph 4, there is also a reference there in the second sentence of the first paragraph: "As for Pasalic and his staff (Ramic et cetera), he and most of his staff have been pro-HVO for a long time. We shall see whether this was under duress or willingly." Your Honours, going back now to document 124 on the first page again, second to last paragraph on that page, starting with, "I was also invited by a number of Bosnian associations in Switzerland and Germany to speak to their associations", there are other documents that I will take your Honours to subsequently which will relate to this question of speeches that would have been undertaken by the accused, Mr. Delalic, but the part that I wish to go to at the moment is the last sentence, which says: "I therefore explained all our mission and plans to Edib Saric and the others." Your Honours, in document 130, at page 9 of that document -- the particular document, document 130, is a document which on its face is said to be written by the accused Mucic as former commander of the BH army camp, Celebici, and it is addressed to the 4th Corps staff in Mostar, and it is a report, a lengthy report. It is a report which relates to, amongst other things, the accused Zejnil Delalic, but the point that I wish to just go to in relation to this, your Honours, is that in the last sentence of that report, the very bottom of the page, there is a reference there to Saric. It says: "Under full moral, personal and military responsibility, I state as irrefutable fact that except in retrospect the TG commander Mr. Z Delalic had no knowledge of these events and neither ordered nor approved anything. On the contrary, he criticised me severely, as can be attested by his deputy, Saric, who was present when I talked about it." Your Honours, the reference in our submission to Saric in this document as the deputy to Zejnil Delalic is reflected again in the reference to Saric in the document 124.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: My memory may be faulty, but I have not heard of Saric before in this case. My memory may be very faulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure, your Honours, whether it has been mentioned by other witnesses or in their testimony, but there are a number of documents that we have here that go to it; document 132, perhaps, as your Honour has raised the matter, I might go to that. This is a letter which appears to be written to the President, and it is about the accused Zejnil Delalic. In this letter, on the first page, he describes himself as Edib Saric in the very first sentence. Then he goes on to write about Zejnil Delalic, and sets out a biography there, and the appointment of Zejnil Delalic, at the very bottom of the page. It says in the centre of that page, page 1 of document 132, it makes reference that he has his own companies in Austria, Switzerland, Belgium and Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Does this letter speak of Delalic's connections with Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This letter we are now looking at, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not think it mentions the camp, not this particular letter. There are other references, but this particular document does not refer to that. But the point I was just making there, your Honour, is that this is, in my submission, a reference to the deputy of the Tactical Group 1 commander. The final paragraph, going back now if I may to 124, on the first page, in the final paragraph, the final sentence makes reference to that expression that we have seen a couple of times, "I have been in the war 24 hours a day since last March, having previously abandoned all my businesses abroad." In my submission, your Honours, it is the similarity of language that is a factor which we would suggest goes to -- is another factor which goes to the reliability of this document, because the similarity in the use of expressions is a factor we would submit that your Honours should have regard to. If I could quickly just demonstrate that, in document 144 at page 6 in the centre of the page, if we could possibly have that, please, the very centre paragraph. Your Honours see there that there is a reference to: "March 1992, right up until 22nd November 1992, 2200 hours, I was constantly there in my responsibility, without taking a day off, going anywhere or doing anything else. I was available 24 hours a day, except for a trip to Zagreb at the beginning of March, where I was sent against my will at the request of the supreme command. I was a guest on a television show", which I referred to last time. This was also, I will not take your Honours to it, but I also made reference to similar type expressions in Exhibit 117. Then there is the next sentence: "Except for five days on mission in Zagreb in May 1992." It then goes on, your Honours, in the very last sentence on that page: "I have not moved from the area along the Igman, Pazaric, Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor and Gornji Vakuf line." Your Honours, Exhibit 127, if we could have that one on the screen, please, is an order, signed under the hand of the co-ordinator and for the Territorial Defence and for the HVO commander. It is an order in 3rd June 1992, it is addressed to the BHZTP Railway Company, Konjic main railway junction: "It is ordered to open up railway traffic at the Jablanica, Konjic, Hadzaric section." It relates, in my submission, to -- it has a relationship to the line that is mentioned in Exhibit 124 that I have just shown you. Going over on to the second page of Exhibit 124, if I may, and moving down to the paragraph starting, "at about 1400 hours" on the second page, about a third of the way down the page, it says: "At about 1400 hours, I crossed the border into Austria. Luckily I had a stamp in my passport dated 26th November 1992. On the next day, I had a call on the mobile phone from Saric", Saric being the deputy that I took your Honours to previously, "who used the occasion to explain everything that remained to be explained." Your Honours, in Exhibit 131, at the bottom of 131, and may I have that on the screen, please, yes, the first page, down, the very bottom paragraph there: "Two days later, Mihad Tinic et cetera came to me with a cellular phone, so I immediately tried to call the numbers in Zagreb and Vienna that Zejnil had left me with. I got through and from that day, all the way until the turmoil and our arrests in early December, I talked to him every day, even seven days a week." If your Honour goes to the top of this document, the person that would appear to be writing it describes himself as: "I was the deputy commander to the commander of Tactical Group 1, Zejnil Delalic." As I have made reference to earlier, it is our submission that that person was Edib Saric, which is consistent, when one sees the reference to the phone call in Exhibit 131, and again the existence of the mobile phone and the phone call in that paragraph in Exhibit 124. Going back again to Exhibit 124, in the centre of the page, there is a -- the next paragraph immediately following: "Only a couple of days earlier, Arif Pasalic suggested I should leave the area for a while and recommended a way to do it." Your Honours, in Exhibit 131 -- I am sorry to have to go back again, but 131 -- there is a reference which seems very similar to that in the middle paragraph of 131, in particular: "A Pasalic knew of it and in my presence he warned him of a potential ambush on the way through Herzegovina." There is a reference to providing him with papers: "He personally told me that he was going to travel that night and that Arif believed that he would only be going a day or two later." Your Honours, again going back to 124 in the middle of the page, the next paragraph which has the number 3 in front of it that starts: "According to some Croatian newspapers, I had flown in a helicopter from Kobiljaca, while other papers said I had left for Kresevo." There are, in our submission, a number of references to these Croatian newspaper reports that appear in Exhibit 126 that I had taken your Honours to before. If we could just have the first page of 126, the top paragraph. You have a reference there in the sentence: "Due to the fact that I knew them personally and the fact that the Croatian media wrote and reported that I had gone over to the Chetniks." There is also a reference in document 130, on page 6 of document 130, the third paragraph from the bottom, if I could, please. Firstly there is a reference to the discord: "I am surprised that our leaders do not realise that this discord is well planned within the BH army, planned by both the Chetniks and the headquarters of the Croatian Community. Judging by the media, it is obvious that both the other sides respect Zejnil more than the BH army and it is unfortunately that I, a Croat, must say that." This document, I would indicate, is a document that is said to be written, or is written, by the defendant Mucic. Your Honours, further down, going back now to document 124, if I may, towards the bottom of the page, in the sentence that starts with "(a).", there is a reference there to Arif Pasalic: "Is Arif Pasalic conducting this investigation on your orders or the orders of the Mostar HVO, or on his own?" I have shown your Honours reference to the fact that it is suggested that Arif Pasalic may have been sympathetic to the HVO. I took your Honours to that, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, there is one thing about these documents, the documents you have shown to us so far, show that he had left Konjic on 25th November at 8.00 pm in the evening. There was a criminal charge against him of desertion and it has been given the colour that he had joined the other side and left in a helicopter; he was merely trying to defend himself. How are these documents relevant to the charges against him before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not that aspect of it. I am drawing your attention to these factors because, in our submission, that shows that they are documents that can be relied upon and should properly be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is a criminal charge against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not for that reason. I am doing it to show their indicia of liability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to draw your attention -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The relevance of them, your Honours, relates to other issues. The relevance particularly of this document relates to his position as Tactical Group 1 -- commander of Tactical Group 1, the fact his deputy was Saric, and all I am doing in drawing your Honours' attention to these matters is that it shows this indicia of reliability. Your Honours, some of the documents vary with relevance, but some of the relevance of them is their interdependence on other documents. There are other documents which are, in our submission, much more relevant, but without these documents they may not have that mutual indicia of reliability, because it is the interrelationship which exists between them which we suggest makes them reliable and ought to be therefore accepted into evidence, so true it is that you can pick any one of these documents -- I withdraw that. True it is that you can pick a number of these documents and say, "standing on its own, what is the relevance of this document? Why are you trying to put this into evidence?" The reason is, of course, what we are saying is that some of the things that are said in this document do not appear relevant on their own, but they go to show that there is a consistent pattern of events described, of circumstances, of similar terminology which appear -- which run as a thread through all the documents and makes them, in our submission, reliable and authentic because of this thread that runs through them. If someone says, "these are forgeries" or whatever, or somebody planted them in the premises or any such suggestion, it is curious then that they would have this thread, because one would have to have gone to extraordinary lengths to be able to achieve that objective, particularly getting to the point where you are creating similar phrases and expressions and events. In our submission, all this goes to establish that. Your Honours, we have heard the evidence of Arif Pasalic and he has -- already there have been some documents tendered, the documents tendered from this set of exhibits, which are now exhibits before you, so in our submission that in itself is significant, that Arif Pasalic comes along to testify in these proceedings, he is shown Exhibit 1 37 -- if I could have that please -- which is documents recovered -- document 137 which will appear on your screen momentarily, was a document found at the premises of INDA-BAU. It was found at those premises, so any suggestion that all of this is just a set-up or a forgery or whatever, it is curious, if that is so, that when this document is produced to General Pasalic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can it be made more legible?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Particularly the signature down the very bottom, in fact the bottom part of the document is perhaps the more interesting part, the very last paragraph. When this document, which has been recovered by the Austrian police, from the premises of INDA-BAU, is shown to General Pasalic, he says "yes, that is my document". It is then tendered and becomes an exhibit in the proceedings, so in my submission that is significant in terms of the argument advanced by the Prosecution that these documents are reliable and is an indicia of reliability of the other documents, because the events described in this document, which was recognised by General Pasalic as his document, which was tendered in these proceedings, relates to these criminal charges which he said he was responsible for instigating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is a charge sheet along with that showing the exact charges against him. One was of desertion and the other was of getting someone liquidated, a person bearing a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. So in our submission, a document which has been proved and admitted, we have here -- going back to Exhibit 124 -- a reference to that very issue, the very question of the investigation which General Pasalic attested to, which we submit further enhances the reliability of this particular document. Going to the last page of document 124, the paragraph commencing number 5, at the top of the page, there is a reference in this document to the supreme command general staff, and then the next to be slandered is Sefer, and your Honours have heard and seen lots of documents which have been issued by the chief of the general staff, Sefer Halilovic, and again referred to there and then the next line down, the reference to, "finally Divjak, who is certain to be finished." Again, your Honours have heard in evidence from General Divjak and how General Divjak was with the accused Zejnil Delalic in the latter part of 1992. Your Honours have heard how General Pasalic speaks of also having General Divjak arrested, but for his protection. Your Honours, then there is again a reference to the HVO wanting to frustrate things, and then again one of these similar threads that I spoke of appears, when it says: "I will offer a reward of 10,000 German Marks to anybody who can prove that I have sold a single gun." I refer your Honours to document 144, document 144 on page 3. It is the second to last paragraph, if I may, starting: "I bought 2,000 uniforms", which is another indicia, I say, of this thread, but your Honours see four lines down in the paragraph: "I will give 10,000 German Marks to anyone who can confirm or testify that I sold a single bullet, radio transmitter, gun, shell or anything similar." Not exactly the same words, but about the same topic and expressed almost in the same way. In our submission, that is very significant. Finally, there is again that reference, if we may go back to the final page of Exhibit 124, again that top paragraph, there is a reference there to the 2,000 uniforms, you can see in the second to last line of the first paragraph on the third page of that document. Your Honours, finally, the signature is, in our submission, significant. There is a reference there to "fire", at the very bottom: "Greetings to the homeland." Then it says "fire" and a Bosnian word which I am instructed means fire, and then immediately under is signed, "Zejnil Delalic". Your Honours, this reference to signing off under the name "fire" is, in our submission, also a matter which we say fits into this pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What does "fire" mean in Bosnian language? What would that signify?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The word is "oganj".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Has it any special significance in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I submit, your Honours, that it is a code name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I see. Then why sign, if that is using a code name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know, your Honour. I cannot explain that. All I know is that it is something that emerged by other documents as well, and I can take your Honour immediately to one document. There is a reference to it, I believe, in the video, Exhibit 116. I am just looking through the transcript quickly for that, but there is a reference to it there. There is also -- I cannot see it now, but in Exhibit 126, page 6, at the very bottom of the page, where this document is signed off. On this occasion, we do not see the name Zejnil Delalic simply signed, but the interpretation here is "flame", which must be an interpretation of "fire", but in my submission, your Honours, it is again a reference to this pattern that appears. So, your Honours, there are other factors that I could take your Honours to, but in relation to this document, where we would submit it points to a pattern that runs through all the documents, but these are some of the main examples of that, and in my submission, having regard to all of the evidence your Honours have heard, having regard to the other exhibits that were located at the premises, having regard to the fact that some of those exhibits have already been tendered in evidence and are accepted as authentic documents, that these are more than adequate indicia of reliability such as to permit this document to be admitted into evidence and relied upon and I move that it be tendered and accepted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any observations, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. We object to the admission of this document 124 for two main reasons. First, the issue of reliability and second, the issue of relevance. If I might expand briefly on those two points, I begin by observing that my learned friend speaks of "threads". Earlier, with the Austrian police, we talked about "chains of custody" which fell apart, and now the threads are dangling as well, and soon they will be grasping at straws in this issue, your Honours. My friend refers to document 124 and takes your Honours through at least seven other documents. In so doing, your Honours, he is asking you to compare and juxtapose names, words, phrases, places and events in document 124, which is not in evidence, in comparison with seven other documents which are not in evidence. This, in my submission, amounts to the Prosecutor coming very close to giving evidence in this case. The proper way to proceed is as he did with Exhibit 137, the one he said he showed to General Pasalic, the one that General Pasalic authenticated. The outstanding issue before your Honours is not only authenticity with regard to the provenance of these documents but also authenticity as to the authorship. When my learned friend says that he can interpret code names, he can tell you who Mr. Saric is, last week he compared two documents where in one we saw the name Ramic for months, we know that reference to a family name such as Kuljanin, Mrkajic, not to mention Delalic, can refer to many different people, and for my friend to suggest that he can tell us what a family name or a code name means is beyond the pale. My friend seems to be suggesting that by showing one document to have been authenticated, Exhibit 137 by General Pasalic, necessarily all the documents to which he is referring are authenticated. This is completely fallacious reasoning. It ignores the fact of the burden on the Prosecution to prove all the elements of its documents. The more conventional way to proceed, and I urge the Trial Chamber to insist the Prosecution to proceed in this way, is to call witnesses who can authenticate, who can verify the reliability of documents. To have my friend stand up and take words, phrases and paragraphs out of context, to weave together a thread which can easily be criticised, cannot be relied upon, is not the appropriate way to proceed. In June your Honours did the same thing where the Prosecution opted not to call the proper police officers from Austria; you clearly indicated to them they were not proceeding in the proper fashion. In my submission this amounts to much the same thing without viva voce evidence to verify the reliability of these documents. We are getting nowhere, we are wasting time and I urge your Honours to stop the Prosecution from proceeding in this way. Finally, on authenticity, I repeat there is no proof as to authorship and provenance of documents, and as far as relevancy goes, Exhibit 124 at least does not tend to prove or disprove any issue related to the indictment in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a pleasure coming to court this afternoon to see a conjuror at work. Document number 124 depends upon a number of other documents. It is my submission to you that it is an illusion. Document number 131 is written by a man allegedly called Saric. I draw your Honours' attention to this: please look at the title of the document, "The Adventurer". Approach this document with care. Why is the author of it heading it, "The Adventurer"? Does that suggest to you, as I respectfully submit it should, that it is a document of perhaps less than complete integrity and truth? Secondly, there is no evidence whatever that this document has been produced by the man called Saric. Indeed, there is no evidence at all, in my submission, that this man Saric exists. The same may be said of document 132. There is simply no evidence whatever that this is produced by a man called Saric. It is a document that might properly be described as flimsy. Of course, the danger is that we are introducing into evidence documents written by people who simply are not witnesses in the case. That gives, at the very best, this document and the other document allegedly written by Saric, zero weight, in my respectful submission. Then we come to the railway document. Your Honours may feel that the link between that document and document 124 could, at its very highest, be described as tenuous. Document 130, a document alleged -- which the Prosecution asserts is written by the defendant Mucic; there is no evidence, no evidence at all, that this document was produced by Mucic. As against him, at the very least, it is not relevant, it is not probative, in the absence of any proof that it is his document. In my respectful submission, that document in particular should not be admitted. When you look at those criticisms that I have, and I invite your Honours to listen with care to what my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan has said, when you take those defects, it can properly be described as an illusion that you are invited to take on board, a great conjuring trick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot help but be struck by an almost Alice in Wonderland kind of contrast between Friday morning and what we have been doing since then. Friday morning a man was brought here, at great expense, from the Bosnian government to authenticate documents for you, which he was only able to do, he said, if he could see the colour of the ink that stamped them and if he could make himself familiar with the signatures that were on them and otherwise independently verify that those documents were authentic. That was seen as an important process, both by the Office of the Prosecutor and by this court, I believe. Then after having had some lunch, all of a sudden we seem to have entered a new world, where documents with absolutely no indication of authenticity at all, no custodian, no nothing, are just being floated around the courtroom with the argument that there are threads between them that somehow give them so authenticity. Most of them are unsigned, most of them purport to be addressed to someone, but none of those someones have appeared here and said "yes, I received such a letter". Many, many times in my own life, and I am sure this is true of virtually everyone in the room, I have sat in my office or in my home and I have written; I have written letters that I have never sent, I have written stories. I enjoy writing, and I would hate that at some point, someone would take those musings of mine and suggest that there is some authenticity to them with regard to facts. Some of the letters that I have written in anger and never sent, for instance, sometimes were not as factual as they might have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I hope they were not letters to the judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No letters to the judges, your Honour, along that line. I have always, I think, had good enough sense to tear them up before I sent them. It seems to me that letters, orders, things of that nature, really do not take on any kind of evidentiary quality unless there is proof you actually sent them to someone, because otherwise you might just be writing for your own amusement. That is what we are seeing here. We are seeing documents without foundation, documents without authenticity, documents that may or may not have meaning and it is like gathering up someone's garbage from outside their house and bringing it in here and saying, "after we have brought someone to tell you about the colour of seals on documents so you can be certain they are important, we have this black bag of garbage that we would also like you to consider". I just think it is outrageous. This is not the way evidence should be presented to a court. What is happening here is even if somewhere down the road you agree that this is not the way evidence should be presented to the court, Mr. Niemann is doing a splendid job and I commend him for standing here reading it all to you so that even if you decide that it should not be before you, you will have heard it, and you will know what is in it. I think this needs to be stopped. I do not think it is proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a slightly different tack, limiting my remarks just to this particular exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate that these documents are not sought to be admitted against Mr. Moran's client.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: We are going to have some limited admissibility, none of these documents are going to be admitted against my client? Any of the documents, or just this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly this document is not admitted against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not say that it does not prove anything one way or the other as to anyone, as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may reply to a couple of these points, firstly, it is very convenient for the Defence to stand up and tell you how it is essential that the only way these documents can ever be admitted in these proceedings is to call the author, when they know that the author is their clients and they know that there is no way the Prosecution can ever call them, so they are then proceeding to tell you, "this evidence never gets before any courts anywhere in the world because the Prosecution can never call the author of the document if he is an accused person, so simply the court is deprived of that evidence". That your Honour, in my submission, is as much Alice in Wonderland as they would ever suggest anything that I am doing here is. Indeed, garbage in the garbage tin could be extremely valuable evidence if it is relevant and relevant to the issue in decision. Maybe hair samples, there may be blood, there may be a knife, a bullet, a gun, there may be anything in the garbage bin which may well be relevant and would be admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do not take him literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sure that they wish to be taken literally. But, your Honours, these are not documents that were found in the garbage bin. These are documents that were filed on the premises and found on the premises in an orderly fashion, as if they were not intended to be thrown in the garbage bin. Certainly we all may from time to time write something which we do not intend, which perhaps is inaccurate, that can be shown in my submission. The matters that I am drawing your Honours' attention to is the fact that these documents are consistent with the balance of the evidence. They are consistent and because they are consistent they are in our submission reliable. These are factors which are the indicia of reliability and make them properly admissible. So, your Honours, in our submission it does not assist, if that is what Mr. Ackerman is doing, because it has not been asserted again that Exhibit 124 was admitted against his client, to say that these may be just musings that have been written down. One often sees in cases diaries admitted against accused persons which are often generated in a similar way, where the contents of the diaries can be extremely relevant and admissible. In my submission, it does not assist to relate these to that sort of writing. These documents can be seen from their face to relate to the topic at hand, they relate to the issue at hand. They are a variety of documents, some of them are at a more formal stage than others, others may only be drafts, but your Honours, in my submission they are not garbage in the garbage can, they are in fact relevant, admissible and it is entirely proper for me to make submissions to you about a thread of consistency that runs through them in order to demonstrate their authenticity. In my submission, your Honours, this document, Exhibit 124 should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, though my learned colleague has already explained our general objections, may I add a few specific objections, since my learned colleague Mr. Niemann has commented on them already?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do object to this. Are we going to have both sides of the Defence get up and make submissions about these things? If that is going to be the case, I think the idea of the Prosecution closing its case before the end of the year is a very faint possibility. Every time I make a submission, I do not have my colleagues here all hop up and give us their views on it, which I am sure they could do and they would be very helpful. We constrain ourselves, and I would ask that the Defence be constrained in a similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I respect your decision that two of us should never comment on the same point, but I wished to make a few remarks in connection with the new points raised by the Prosecution, and if I may be allowed, I will do that. If not, I will refer to other documents, but I will not be repeating the things that my learned friend Mr. O'Sullivan said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have always said, the rules of debate do not allow a ding-dong practice. I think there is a limit, so I think maybe your submissions are over. That was the reply. If you think, after that reply, you also should be entitled to speak, that is not right. One counsel is on his or her feet; you must put the arguments the way you think you could do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague O'Sullivan has said everything that was necessary in connection with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think you have go on with a criticism, because I think it is enough to challenge every aspect of the Prosecution's presentation. That is all for the time being? We will reserve our ruling until later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the record be clear that there was no offer of this document against Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How many times will that be said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, sometimes I get a little nervous about those things. I apologise if I am beating a dead horse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose so. It might not arise again. All right, I think it has been said sufficiently. What next do you have for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have more of the documents, your Honour. I have many more of these documents, your Honour. I do not know of any other way to reduce the amount of time it takes to deal with them. These are documents that were found on the premises and we seek to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can go ahead. It is your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Might I move on to the next document, Exhibit 124. Might that be displayed -- sorry, 125. Might that be displayed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this is displayed, I want to rise to object to its even being displayed. This document deals with a matter that Mr. Niemann -- I understand that is what it deals with, that Mr. Niemann had agreed as late as last week was not material to this case, and did not have any business coming before this court. I do not know if I am confused about the document or not. Let me just look at it. (Pause). I have reason to believe that this refers to the Bubalo matter which we had basically agreed not to get into and it was not appropriate to come before the court. That is why I am objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position is, and has been, and has not changed, is that we are not seeking to rely on the document for any other purpose than the fact that it relates to or goes to prove the reference to the position held by the accused Delalic and Mucic. We are not seeking to rely on it or to introduce into these proceedings any other aspect of the matter. We would ask your Honours to disregard any other reference to it, but it has not been the case at all that there was an agreement that it would not be tendered into evidence. It was agreed, and Mr. Moran particularly is aware of this, it was agreed to be tendered into evidence on the limited basis that we argue that the persons in authority who went to create these documents, including General Pasalic, who already discussed a document which is now an exhibit, ought to have known the rank and position held by the persons, by the accused persons Delalic and Mucic, and that therefore it has that indicia of reliability. This particular document is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know if you are finished responding to my argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please let him finish responding, but I have an additional something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With this particular document, your Honours, we say it is relevant for the very limited purpose that it goes to show the thread of documents in relation to this point. It is merely a link in that chain, a link in that thread of documents which we say in combination establish the reliability of the documents in toto. In other words, it is merely a small part of that mosaic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no objection, other things being established, that is reliability, authenticity and relevance, to an offer for the purpose which Mr. Niemann has suggested that it be offered for. The way I have seen that handled and the best way I think to handle it is to take a permanent black marker and redact from the document all those things that the Prosecution does not intend it to be offered for, because there are judicial officers beyond this Trial Chamber who might be studying these documents for whatever purpose they might be studying them, with relation to my client Mr. Landzo in the future. I have no question, but what this particular Trial Chamber, this particular panel of three judges would clearly be able to separate in their own minds what the document is being offered for from the other things contained therein. I cannot say the same about future judges who might be making decisions with regard to documents in this case, so the safe way to deal with it is for the Prosecutor to take a permanent black marker and on the copy going into evidence redact everything they do not mean to be offering it for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I find, your Honour, this is an extraordinary submission having regard to the document, bearing in mind in particular that Exhibit 137 has been admitted in unredacted form into evidence. It relates to the very question -- this particular document is a decision of the public prosecutor that all charges against the accused Zejnil Delalic and Zdravko Mucic are dropped, so why my friend would now stand up and say that some judge may be misled by it is an extraordinary submission in my view, your Honours. I would have thought that if anything else, they would have demanded that this document be admitted into evidence. But as I say, your Honour, we are not seeking to put it into evidence in order that it be evidence to the fact that the charges against Mucic and Delalic are dropped. We say whether they were dropped is irrelevant, because, your Honours, we are not tendering any of these documents so that your Honours would have regard whatsoever to the criminal charges, but, your Honours, if Mr. Ackerman is now telling you that he is concerned about other judges reading it and thinking that these gentlemen may have been accused of some charges and that that for some reason or another may be a bad thing. I find it extraordinary that he would stand up and object to the tender of this document, which achieves the very objective that he is concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann may be right, it may be extraordinary, but it also is consistent. When Exhibit 137 was offered, I believe that I objected very strenuously to those portions of it which I felt were irrelevant and I believe that I suggested at that time that they should be redacted, and trying to be consistent, I think I am right and I think with regard to 137, that language should also be redacted from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, whether or not it is redacted, I do believe that your Honours are perfectly capable of ignoring the references in there to the charges as such, and accepting this document on the very limited basis that we submit it should be accepted into evidence under, and that is it goes to the mosaic of documents that are relevant in order to establish their position that I have referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have listened to your arguments. This is not a reply to what Mr. Ackerman said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will then proceed, your Honour, to examine the document, if your Honour pleases. Perhaps it could be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, I take it that my objection and my suggestion on redaction is overruled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is on record. We will examine it. It depends on what we do with the exhibit itself. You have suggested it should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My suggestion was it should be redacted before it was displayed to your Honours, so only the portions that the Prosecution is offering would be displayed to your Honours, since you sit as finders of fact, and with regard to future judicial bodies who may be considering this evidence. I just want the record to show whether or not my objection in that regard has been sustained or overruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I do not think it is really necessary for the purposes of this case. If the argument is for other cases or for other readers such redaction is necessary, I suppose it might be, but for our own purposes, I do not think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am talking about perhaps the Appellate Chamber, your Honour, or perhaps a future judicial body that might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you sure your objection will not be on record?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it probably is on record and I think now your Honours' view of that objection is on record, so I have probably made my record, I can sit down and be quiet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it is not redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to document 125 that appears on the screen, on the original Bosnian version of that document, it is a typewritten document, it bears a seal on the bottom of the document, and it appears to be signed. In our submission, your Honour, it has all the appearance of a formal document of the type that your Honours have seen. It is a document that was found on the premises of INDA-BAU --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. It was a mistake to have actually asked you to continue, because I think we should be going for a short break. But before we go, I think when we return at 4.30, we might like to take on the arguments on the motion for leave to call Witness V. I do not know whether the Defence is aware of that motion, the motion for protective measures. I think in addition the motion to call Witness J. I do not think it will take too long. We will go for a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, can we hear you on your motions? Who is presenting it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Ms McHenry will be arguing it for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I will not be long, your Honours. I believe the bases for our motions have been set out in our written pleadings, which were filed on Friday and given to the Defence Friday afternoon. Our first two motions concern Witness V, a security officer in the Tribunal. We first seek leave to call Witness V, his name was not on the initial witness list because we had not planned on calling Witness V at the time we filed our witness list. In the middle of October, there were some issues that came to Witness V's attention which we think is admissible and relevance for the case in chief. It may also be separately grounds for contempt that your Honours may also hear at the same time, but the present motion is with respect to its relevance as to the case in chief. With respect to Witness V we have also filed a motion seeking that his identity be kept secret from the public and media because this security officer has worked in Bosnia and wishes to do so in the near future. I believe he has some prospects in that regard and he believes if his identity were known it could affect his ability to obtain and perform his job. Thus he has indicated that he will only testify if his identity can be protected from the public and media. We have also a motion for protective measures for Witness J. He is a witness who has already testified, who heard certain remarks made by the accused which we think again is relevant evidence at trial. The witness, who was already a vulnerable witness, is traumatised and has indicated that he does not wish to be in the same room with the accused again. Thus he seeks permission to testify using the remote witness room. There would be no restrictions on the rights of the accused or Defence counsel to view the witness. That is not what he seeks protection from. Your Honour, I believe the testimony of both witnesses will be very short, but nonetheless, we are requesting it as relevant evidence for the reasons stated in our motions. Unless your Honours have any questions, that concludes my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have we given you permission to recall Witness J?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I believe Mr. Niemann spoke to that on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You must seek permission to recall Witness J, then the other thing will arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has been discharged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: In that case, your Honour, may I amend our motion to make also an oral motion to recall Witness J. I am sorry, I thought Mr. Niemann mentioned this, that we did not need to do so, but I would seek leave to orally request leave to call Witness J with respect to the matters that I believe everyone knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Why do you want to recall Witness J?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Because we believe the evidence concerning the alleged threat made to Witness J is direct evidence of consciousness of guilt and therefore that it is admissible evidence. It is the case in many systems that threats to a witness, as well as flight of an accused, are both, in addition to potentially being criminal offences in their own right, are evidence of consciousness of guilt. In particular, we believe that the reason that the accused have threatened the witnesses is because they do not want these witnesses to testify, because they realise that their truthful testimony will convict them, so we believe it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The accused gave the threat while the witness was appearing in the witness box or before that? Before he appeared in the court?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the threat was during the witness's testimony, and we believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The witness had already come, so issuing a threat, how would that prove his guilt?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it could certainly intimidate the witness, it could upset the witness, it could prevent him from coming back into the courtroom, all those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is intimidating a witness; that is a contempt. Those are separate proceedings, contempt proceedings. How is it relevant to the Celebici case?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is the contention of the Prosecution, your Honours, and in many legal systems, that threatening a witness, including while he is giving evidence, is evidence of consciousness of guilt. Had it occurred after the witness had finished, then it may be that there would be less evidence, but certainly it can be inferred that the accused were trying to intimidate the witness from either being so upset that he was unable to present a credible appearance, or such that he would refuse to come into the courtroom again, or upsetting him so that he would be too afraid to answer truthfully the additional questions that were being put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Was his examination-in-chief over, or was it before that he issued the threat?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Examination in chief was over, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So he had testified what he wanted to say. How would a subsequent threat --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly believe cross-examination counts as evidence too, and so the fact that it was during cross-examination the Prosecution does not believe is of any legal significance to whether or not the evidence is consciousness of guilt or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you will be able to call him if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was rather hoping your Honours might invite some comments from the Defence on the motion before deciding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you could. I am just putting you on notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a favourite trick of prosecuting counsel, and I sometimes act in that capacity myself, that when you do not have terribly much, you pick up a piece of mud and throw it. Your Honours, this is a peripheral irrelevant issue which is not probative of any fact or issue. This consciousness of guilt thing is preposterous and I would invite your Honours to reject this application.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just limited to Witness V, I find it most incredible that an employee of the United Nations will sit there and tell a court that is an arm of the Security Council of the United Nations that the only way he is going to testify is if he is granted some kind of anonymity. Your Honour, this guy -- protection of witnesses' identities I think has been overdone, and the court knows my feelings on that, but to take someone who is presumably an armed security guard for the United Nations in The Hague and to say that maybe because he will go back to Bosnia some day we are going to let him testify anonymously, and have him say to the court through the Prosecutor essentially that he will not appear unless he can testify anonymously -- anonymously to the world, not as to the court or participants -- to me is absolutely incredible. I think the Blaskic Appellate Decision was handed down last week and Judge Karibi-Whyte, you can correct me on this, if I am overstating or understating what the Appellate Chamber held, but basically you held this Tribunal is an arm of the Security Council. To me it is incredible that if the Security Council summoned Koffi-Anan to a meeting and said, "We want to hear what you have to say about this", if Koffi-Anan refused, he would have substantial problems remaining the Secretary General of the United Nations. To have an employee of the Tribunal itself put some kind of conditions like this on his testimony is just absolutely mind-boggling. If there is anybody that should be testifying, should not have any real fear of testifying, it is a security guard for the United Nations. We have had citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina testifying here for the Prosecution with their names and their faces spread all over television and all over the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think this is really strange. When the Rules were being established, not only the Rules but the Articles of the Tribunal themselves were being established, they were conscious of the possibility of a witness being afraid of the security. If you look at the provisions, they are very clear, Article 20 is very clear about that. They did not even select whether you are an United Nations official or you are a private person. Everybody who feels genuinely and justifiably frightened of his security could be accorded such privileges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have already done that in the Dokmanovic case, his arrest has been challenged by the Defence and we gave protection to one of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just -- again, the Tribunal is well aware of my feelings about public testimony, just to me this is -- Judge Karibi-Whyte, you said "justifiable fears". What we have to be careful about is we do not let a witness -- I can think of one witness off the top of my head who said that he had real fears and was terrified if he testified publicly he would face some kind of problems and the next thing you know we were watching him on television. I am not saying that this person will do that, but we have to look at the justifiableness of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We do not want to exaggerate the nature of the persons being tried. Nobody wants to play down or exaggerate their capabilities, so when somebody says he is afraid, and especially for things said to his hearing, you do not take it as if it is a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem and I am not objecting to Witness J testifying however he wants to testify. My comments are limited solely to Witness V, and the reasonableness of any perceived fears he may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose so. He is also a frightened man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you may know more about that than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am only relying on what was put here. I know nothing outside what is in the motions. I have no particular personal knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Like I said, my feeling is that the Trial Chamber should make an individualised determination of the reasonableness of these kinds of fears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I agree, especially when threats come from inside, from an accused person directly. I think one should take it seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know if there is any evidence that this security guard was threatened by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose they are fears associated by what had been threatened to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course this remains a fact issue for the Trial Chamber to decide and I am just suggesting that it is a fact issue that the Trial Chamber should face and should look at the reasonableness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: -- of the fears as it applies, especially to this one individual person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly on behalf of Mr. Delalic, we take the position that this matter is not connected to the indictment and we oppose any further delays in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the issue with regard to Witness V is directly relevant to my client Mr. Landzo and no one else, and so I think it is probably appropriate that I say something about this motion. It appears that we are having a very hard time getting to the end of this case, and one of the reasons are collateral matters like this that seem to side-track us now and then. I think this is clearly a collateral matter, has no business being brought before this Trial Chamber at this point in time. The basic question that the Trial Chamber must ask with regard to Witness V and the testimony he proposes to give is whether or not he is here to give evidence that is relevant to any part of the indictment in this case. Relevant evidence is most often defined as evidence likely to make an issue of consequence to the determination of the issues before the Tribunal, of consequence to answering the questions that are contained in the indictment. The Office of the Prosecutor suggest to you, both in writing and orally, that the relevance of this evidence, in other words what it is about this evidence that makes it relevant, is that it is evidence of consciousness of guilt. I find that preposterous. I do not know of a jurisdiction where this kind of evidence would be viewed as evidence of consciousness of guilt. Flight evidence in my country is admitted for that purpose. That is where a defendant tries to flee from an impending arrest, a defendant knows that he has been indicted and tries to flee that indictment. I agree, that can be evidence of consciousness of guilt. This is an incredible stretch, to suggest to you that whether or not -- that this alleged evidence, whether or not it is true, is evidence of consciousness of guilt. It can be equally evidence of consciousness of innocence. It has exactly the same quality on either side, and that is why it has no chance whatsoever of making any issue before this Tribunal more or less probable. It is just a waste of your time, it is just a way to keep this case from finally coming to a conclusion by spending a day or two dealing with this collateral matter. We had previously filed a motion asking for a hearing on it, because we thought that that hearing should be held out of fear that you would consider the memorandum that came to you from the Registry as evidence. We have now realised that that was in error, that you clearly would not consider it as evidence unless someone took the next step to formally bring it before you, and that would largely have to be done by your Honours, based upon whether you felt that was necessary or not. So I think at this point the effort to further delay the conclusion of this proceeding by bringing in a matter collateral, on the dubious suggestion that it is evidence of consciousness of guilt, is improper and I think you should reject it and we should get on with Mr. Niemann's presentation of documents, and then on to the balance of the witnesses that are scheduled to appear before you in this case. Thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I am not too sure whether I am speaking for more than myself here. What we have before us now are applications for motion to call Witness V, and then another one, protection for Witness V, and then another application to call Witness J. I agree perhaps after that the Prosecution might consider giving us why they now want to call these witnesses. There is nothing like any particular offence before us, there is nothing like that, and much of what you have recounted perhaps might be what the Prosecution has in mind, but we are not too sure whether that is what will result from all this exercise. So at this stage, we are only concerned with the application before us; that is whether these witnesses should be called, and the protection we should give to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Prosecution has made it quite clear why they want to call these two witnesses. It has to do with statements allegedly made by Mr. Landzo and Mr. Mucic which have been set out in a memorandum that came to you from the Registrar. They have not indicated they have any other purpose in calling these witnesses, and I have therefore directed my remarks regarding the irrelevancy of this evidence to the contents of the memorandum that you received from Madam de Sampayo, regarding the report of a security guard as to what Mr. Landzo said on a certain date during the testimony or during a break. I do not think the Prosecution intends to call them for any other purpose, so I think it is rather clear what that purpose is and I think the Prosecutor would agree with me that is what that purpose is. That is not a secret. Rather than go through the exercise of saying, "okay, we are going to grant the motion" and then later hear an argument as to why the witness should not be heard and say, "you are right, we are not going to hear the witness", seems to take up even more of this Tribunal's time. I was hoping all of those issues could be dealt with right now, get it over with, and we would know whether or not we are going to be facing these witnesses tomorrow. I do not think we should be, I do not think it is proper, I do not think it is relevant, I think it is collateral.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman has correctly stated the reasons the Prosecution is calling these witnesses. It is to provide evidence as is accurately recounted in the Registrar's memorandum. The Prosecution does believe this is relevant evidence for this trial in that it is evidence of consciousness of guilt and I will not repeat my arguments here, but that is why the Prosecution is seeking to call them, and to the extent that at least one witness is coming from a long distance, we do not disagree with Mr. Ackerman that it is acceptable for your Honours to decide it now, whether or not this is -- if in fact the witnesses come and testify consistent with the memorandum, whether or not that is relevant evidence. We do not object to that, and Mr. Ackerman has correctly stated why the Prosecution is calling them, and I will not repeat the Prosecution's argument as to why this is relevant evidence for the trial, but the Prosecution does believe it is relevant evidence for this trial, and as everyone agrees, it may also be supplementary evidence of contempt. But the issue now is with respect to the trial, so we would be seeking to call them as evidence in its case in chief for the charges against these accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will rise for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has, as quickly as we could, gone into the issue. We find that there is no juridical basis for calling these witnesses. If the other arguments which we think might even be more contentious for calling these witnesses have been considered, the proper procedure for doing so can be undertaken. We are not too satisfied that merely calling witnesses at this stage to give evidence of consciousness of guilt for what was said is not the ideal way to proceed against matters of this nature. So we do not think we can grant the applications which are before us. Have you anything to say about the applications?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. We thank you for making such a quick ruling on this so we did not have to bring the witnesses as evidence in our case in chief. We will anticipate bringing these witnesses at another time as evidence of contempt, but there is no reason to do it at the present time, so we will just defer that and talk to the witnesses about their schedules and everything else and then bring it separately. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, we thought about that, and we felt perhaps there are procedures for bringing the real offence which was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just should indicate, your Honours, that we may not either. We may decide not to take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps it might even be better if you did not. We refuse your applications. Now we will hear you on your applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. Your Honours, the last document we were looking at was Exhibit 125, and perhaps if that can be displayed on the screen. Your Honours, when this particular document was shown to Mr. Moerbauer in his evidence at page 3653, lines 11 and 12, Officer Moerbauer said: "This document was in the binder I5. It was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at the police headquarters, Vienna." It was also a document that was shown to the witness Pasalic in the course of his evidence. Your Honours, the Prosecution's application to tender this document is merely on the limited basis that it is part of the series of documents which deal with this particular issue, and it is not sought to be tendered as truth of the contents of any aspect of it that relates to whether or not the accused, Delalic and Mucic, were in any way guilty of the offences that are alleged therein. Indeed, in our submission, your Honour, the reference to the offences as such is not a matter which is relied on by the Prosecution, so it is tendered -- sought to be tendered on a very limited basis. It does have a relationship, as I say, your Honours, to the whole range of other documents. I will not take your Honour to every one of them, but I am able to list them, where it is our submission that there is a relationship to them in the mosaic of documents that are tendered. Firstly Exhibit 117 which your Honours have already looked at, but further in Exhibit 145, which is a document which was again found on the premises, and simply is a reference to -- makes reference to the article of desertion under the Criminal Code, Article 217, relating to desertion. Your Honours can see that, there is the article as set out there in part. If your Honours look at the exhibit I am referring to, Exhibit 125, there is a reference there in that article, so the Prosecution seek to tender -- second line, top of the page, there is reference to Article 217. The Prosecution seek to tender it as it is part of a series of documents, others which are far more relevant than this document, and as I say, it has indicia of reliability because of the fact that it fits into this pattern. But we go further and say it is a more formal looking document than others I have referred to, because it has a reference there to -- it has a stamp there, which we have seen from other evidence tends to be characteristic of a lot of the documents which we have examined. I move that that document be accepted into evidence. As your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Delalic objects to this document being admitted into evidence for the reasons already given, but since my learned colleague Mr. Niemann has given me the opportunity to go back to some of those arguments, allow me to present them. First of all, I should like to remind you, your Honours, that discussing the exhibits allegedly seized in INDA-BAU on 9th June already, my learned friend Mr. Turone, in response to a comment on your part, said that for the Prosecutor to prove that a certain document comes from a certain premise, that he would call Mr. Navrat and Mr. Unger. In line with that, your Honours, Judge Karibi-Whyte clearly stated that if the Prosecutor fails to prove each of these elements then not a single of those exhibits would be admitted into evidence. You stated this on 9th June, on page 3647 of the transcript. Later, in your ruling of 25th September, in response to our submission that the value of some documents was being prejudged, you clearly said that the Prosecutor has to prove each of the elements of the case, which means that this Trial Chamber never ruled on the authenticity of these documents. Therefore there are no exhibits that have been proven to have come from the INDA-BAU premises. The Prosecutor has not still proven that any of the offered documents came from the INDA-BAU premises. Witness Navrat, called by the Prosecution, could not recognise a single one of those documents, nor did he mark any of those documents. Therefore, it would be essential for the Prosecutor, when tendering a document into evidence in this court, he should prove where the document comes from, who was its author, and only then to discuss its possible relevance and probative value. However, with respect to document 125, we encounter another problem, whereby the Prosecutor is trying to show you all these documents were in one place, that they are authentic and that they are linked to one another, as he has tried to say with respect to document 124, claiming that there was a thread that testifies to its reliability. This document, on the dropping of charges against Zejnil Delalic and Zdravko Mucic, is a public document and it can be admitted anywhere. As Judge Jan has already noted, many phrases from the other documents tell the story on criminal proceedings against my client and Mr. Mucic. Therefore, to link to a public document several pieces of paper, unauthenticated papers out of the 2,700 bits of paper found in several places, allegedly, in Vienna and Munich, is not a way to prove the reliability of these documents, nor to prove that these documents come from the premises where they are said to have come from. Therefore the authenticity of these documents remains contested, and I think to rely on the thread indicated by the Prosecutor will not lead this court to ignore Rule 89 and Rule 95, according to which a fair trial would be in jeopardy if these documents, documents of this kind, were to be admitted. The next point I wish to make is something that my colleagues have already referred to, and that is that an unauthenticated and unreliable document is being proven with the help of other unauthenticated and unreliable documents, and not with documents as a whole, but with sentences taken out of context. In the story as presented before this court, they are intended to show consistency and to lead us to the conclusion that all these documents are reliable and relevant. Let me, your Honours, draw attention to a technical point. Each time an exhibit is shown to you it is put on the monitor and you see the English translation of that document. I should like to ask my colleagues to put the next documents in the original, and then you will see that these are not documents, these are notes scribbled by various persons whose handwriting was never proven, and which can come from various sources. I would like to refer to the testimony of a witness here when we were talking about the possibilities as to which document was in which folder. The arguments I have already presented that were confirmed by the Prosecutor, and that is the appointment of the 11th, which was allegedly from Vienna, and that it was shown to my client. This is quite incorrect, because what my client was shown was another document with a fax number and this can easily be verified. It is number 1290 and if we review this method of presentation of all documents, including a public document which can be found with the Defence counsel or various people who may have tried to participate in the propaganda or counter-propaganda against my client, and if it is not found to have come from a premises belonging to my client, then the reliability of that document, as well as the reliability of the assertion that it comes from that premises, can also be contested. The risk of linking these documents with other unreliable documents is obvious. If we just go back to the previous document, when the name Saric was discussed and later the name Edib Saric, instead of the Prosecutor relying on the evidence presented in this Trial Chamber and which clearly showed the unreliability of document 124, we are being offered elements of unidentified, unauthenticated and highly problematic other documents. Namely, we are coming to the end of the case in chief, we have heard a great deal of testimony. When General Pasalic saw document 124, he immediately noted and said clearly that on 8th December, Tactical Group no longer existed. This same witness confirmed the report he sent to the supreme command and which indicated the position of Edib Saric, of whom we do not know whether he exists and what he is doing. When shown other documents, the witness confirmed as valid those documents. That same witness, General Pasalic, established that Edib Saric was appointed deputy commander of Tactical Group 2, and this has nothing to do with Mr. Delalic or with Tactical Group 1. Also, another document has been admitted into evidence which clearly shows that Edib Saric, if all the Prosecutor wanted to refer to him in support of this thin thread of consistency, we see from that document that Edib Saric is a liaison officer in a temporary command of the group JUG. Therefore the evidence that we heard, with the help of a witness whose testimony we heard, is real proper evidence on the basis of which we can verify the validity of these documents. Bits of paper with problematic translations which we were unable to compare because some of the writing is quite illegible is not a way to prove the reliability or relevance of any document. I have said all this referring to a document which may be official and is not disputed, but what is disputed is that the Prosecutor in this case, as in all others, could not prove where it came from, the source of that document, because Navrat could not recognise this document. For these reasons and the reasons we presented earlier, I propose that this document, as well as the previous one, not be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just quickly respond? One at a time I think might be easier. Your Honours, the issue of whether or not there was a search of the premises and whether the documents were legally seized has been dealt with and disposed of by your Honours. I note what Madam Residovic has said about this being a public document and could be admitted anywhere and I rely on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission there are three problems the Prosecution have. I note what my learned friend has said about my learned friend Ms. Residovic's comments. Firstly, this document lacks any form of relevance or probative value. It is not probative of any fact or issue in my submission. Secondly, as far as the quality of the document is concerned, it is asserted that it is a public document.
