Your Honour, a number of remarks are made by my learned friend, and I will return to those in a moment, about the quality of the document. Of course, as my learned friend Mr. Ackerman said earlier on this afternoon, on Friday we had the keeper of documents, custodian of documents, come and prove public documents. The Prosecution, and this is their third problem in my submission, does it on this occasion in a quite different way. When we assert the Prosecution has to prove a document, we did not have in mind that counsel for the Prosecution would be giving evidence as to the provenance of the document. What my learned friend has said is this: it is typewritten, it bears a seal at the bottom of the document, it appears -- note that word, "appears" to be signed -- it has all the appearance of a formal document of the type that your Honours has seen. Then a moment or two ago, he said: "It is a more formal looking document than others I have referred to because it has a stamp there which we have seen from other evidence tends to be characteristic of a lot of the documents we have examined." Your Honour, in my submission it is not right that counsel for the Prosecution should give evidence and say, "this is an authentic document"; that is for others to give evidence about and prove. That is why they had the keeper of records here last Friday. So in my respectful submission, there is no evidence that this document is a genuine one, not least because he asserts it has a stamp on it: there are very many people out there in the world who are very skilled at producing such stamps, and in my country during the Second World War, there was a whole army of them in prisoner of war camps doing precisely that; fooling our German friends up hill and down dale. That is why you have to prove the document, you have to prove that it has a genuine stamp. That is why you call the keeper of records to say, "I recognise this as a genuine stamp". It is not for counsel for the Prosecution to give evidence and do it instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Very quickly, it seems to be -- two things seem to be asserted. One is that I am giving evidence, which is not true. What I am doing is taking your Honours to the documents. The documents speak for themselves. It is entirely appropriate for counsel to refer to what a document says and show your Honours by reference to the document what is being said or what it shows. This is well known by counsel. Secondly, your Honours, it seems to be argued that there is only one way that a document can be admitted into evidence and one way only, and that if the Prosecution does not proceed pursuant to that one way then that is the end of the matter, the thing is not admitted. This document is not in the possession of the keeper of records; this document was found at the premises in INDA-BAU. Your Honours, it is the fact that it was found at the premises of INDA-BAU, which is a piece of evidence which the Prosecution considers to be a very important part of the evidence. You do not bring -- if the original of the document was there, your Honours would say, quite rightly, "what is the relevance of this document?" It is because of where it was found; it is because of where it was located, because of its relationship to other documents, that makes it relevant and admissible and important, in our submission. So it is not correct to simply say, "the only way it can be done is to call the keeper of records". On its own, in isolation, calling the keeper of records, your Honours would have a very legitimate question; "why are you trying to put this into evidence?" In my submission, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me find out exactly the proposal of entering these documents as exhibits. Is it for the authenticity of the documents or the content of what the documents themselves represent?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the highly significant aspect of them is what they say and where they were. It is just the same as what often happens in so many cases that your Honours will be familiar with, where the police go in and execute a search warrant at the premises of a person who is subsequently charged with an offence. There is a whole range of things. One might be, in a drug case, tendering a set of scales. A set of scales might be an innocent kitchen appliance used for baking cakes or something, or it could be a basis upon which people weigh out heroin or some other form of drugs. Just simply saying that you need the manufacturer of the scales to come along to tender them is a nonsense. It is where they are found that is the significant aspect of it and their contents, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we have had enough for today. We should continue tomorrow morning at 10.00, if you still have more documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have more documents, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How many more?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About 20, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you sure you have not covered the ground yet for which these documents might be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can assure you I would be delighted to simply tender them in one exercise and it be over with, but I fear that is not going to be possible. I have to deal with them individually, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

procedural_notes.text: (Court adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
